content: The Cercozoa are a diverse group of protists that include most amoeboid and flagellated organisms which feed using filose pseudopodia. These pseudopodia are thin, thread-like extensions of the cell, and their distribution may be limited to specific areas of the cell surface. Unlike many other protozoa, Cercozoa lack a true cytostome, or mouth, for feeding. Despite their structural diversity, genetic studies strongly support their classification as a unified group. Cercozoa are closely related to Foraminifera and Radiolaria, which are amoeboid organisms typically characterized by their intricate shells. Together, these groups form a larger supergroup known as the Rhizaria. Among the Cercozoa, the euglyphids are particularly well-known. These are filose amoebae that possess shells made of siliceous (silica-based) scales or plates. Euglyphids are commonly found in soil, nutrient-rich aquatic environments, and on the surfaces of aquatic plants. Other filose amoebae within the Cercozoa produce organic shells. These include groups such as the tectofilosids and Gromia. Historically, these organisms were grouped with the euglyphids under the classification Testaceafilosia. However, this grouping is not monophyletic, meaning it does not include all descendants of a common ancestor. Most members of this group, based on genetic studies, are either part of or closely related to the Cercozoa, along with certain flagellates that also possess shells. Another significant subgroup within the Cercozoa is the chlorarachniophytes. These are unusual amoebae that form a reticulating (net-like) structure. They are distinct because they contain chloroplasts, which are thought to have originated from a green alga that was engulfed by the ancestor of these organisms. The chloroplasts in chlorarachniophytes are surrounded by four membranes and retain a vestigial nucleus, known as a nucleomorph. This feature has made chlorarachniophytes a key focus of research into the endosymbiotic origins of organelles. Other notable members of the Cercozoa include the cercomonads, which are flagellates commonly found in soil, and the Phaeodarea, a group of marine protozoa that were previously classified as radiolarians. Additionally, three groups traditionally considered heliozoans—dimorphids, desmothoracids, and gymnosphaerids—are now recognized as part of the Cercozoa. The classification and composition of the Cercozoa remain an area of active research. For example, two parasitic groups, the Phytomyxea and Ascetosporea, as well as the shelled amoeba Gromia, may represent basal members of the Cercozoa, although some phylogenetic trees suggest they are more closely related to the Foraminifera. The spongomonads, once included in the Cercozoa, are now thought to belong to the Amoebozoa. Furthermore, several small and poorly understood groups of protozoa are tentatively classified as Cercozoa, and ongoing research is likely to reveal that many obscure genera also belong to this group.
